Check R4SUB Ecosystem Dependency Compatibility

Source: R/deps.R
r4sub_deps.Rd

Inspects the dependencies that R4SUB ecosystem packages declare on each other and reports whether the versions you have installed satisfy those declarations. This answers a question a meta-package is well placed to answer: "is my installed R4SUB ecosystem internally consistent, or is some member too old for another member that depends on it?"

Usage

r4sub_deps(include_suggests = FALSE)

# S3 method for class 'r4sub_deps'
format(x, ...)

# S3 method for class 'r4sub_deps'
print(x, ...)

Arguments

include_suggests

Logical. If FALSE (default), only hard dependencies (Depends and Imports) are examined. If TRUE, Suggests edges are included as well; these are optional, so an unsatisfied Suggests edge is reported with status "suggested-missing" rather than "missing".

x

An r4sub_deps object, as returned by r4sub_deps().

...

Ignored, for compatibility with the format() and print() generics.

Value

An object of class r4sub_deps (a tibble) with one row per ecosystem-internal dependency edge and the columns:

package

The ecosystem package that declares the dependency.

dependency

The ecosystem package it depends on.

type

"Depends", "Imports", or "Suggests".

required

The declared version constraint (e.g. ">= 0.1.2"), or NA when no version is pinned.

installed

The installed version of dependency, or NA when it is not installed.

status

"ok", "outdated", "missing", or, for optional edges, "suggested-missing".

Returned invisibly; a one-line summary is printed when the function is called, and the full report is produced by the print/format methods.

Details

The check is performed entirely from locally installed package metadata (each package's DESCRIPTION). It performs no network access and does not consult CRAN; it only compares the versions already installed on your machine against the version constraints those packages declare.

Only edges within the R4SUB ecosystem are reported: a dependency on, say, cli or tibble is ignored, because this helper is about ecosystem self-consistency rather than general package management.

The returned object carries the r4sub_deps class, so printing it renders a readable report that lists any outdated or missing ecosystem dependencies. The underlying object is a tibble::tibble(), so it can be filtered, counted, or joined like any other data frame.

Examples

# Report ecosystem-internal dependency compatibility
deps <- r4sub_deps()
#> ✔ All R4SUB ecosystem dependencies satisfied.

# Render the full report (same as printing `deps`)
print(deps)
#> ✔ All R4SUB ecosystem dependencies satisfied.

# Keep only unsatisfied edges
deps[deps$status != "ok", ]
#> ✔ All R4SUB ecosystem dependencies satisfied.
